Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 1.1 Cards and Firework Stacks 1.2 Communication 2 Setup 3 Gameplay 3.1 Give a Clue 3.2 Play a Card 3.3 Discard a Card 4 Game End 4.1 Scoring 5 Variants 5.1 Colors 5.2 Black Powder 5.3 5 Flamboyants 5.4 Convention Used 5.5 Preset Deck 5.6 Unofficial variant Overview Hanabi is a cooperative game where your collective goal is to build a fabulous fireworks show. Like any decent show, you should start with small fireworks and finish with the big ones. You will do this by playing red, yellow, green, blue and white cards from ranks 1 to 5. The problem? You don't know what cards you have. But you know which ones your fellow players do. So you must communicate with each other to build a proper show by placing cards in sequential order with no misfires. Cards and Firework Stacks The deck has 50 cards. The cards come in five colors: red yellow green blue white Each color has 10 cards: 3 card 1 ,with a Hanabi card 1 clue, , 2 card 2 ,with a Hanabi card 2 clue, , 2 card 3 ,with a Hanabi card 3 clue, , 2 card 4 ,with a Hanabi card 4 clue, , 1 card 5 ,with a Hanabi card 5 clue, . There is only one firework stack of each color which start empty. cards in the deck red r yellow y green g blue b white w multicolor m black powder Each firework must be placed in ascending order starting from 1, so you are aiming for cards in the deck red 5 r yellow 5 y green 5 g blue 5 b white 5 w multicolor m black powder . Playing a card on any stack that is not the next number in the sequence will result in a misfire. If three misfires occur, the game is over and the players lose. Communication You communicate with your teammates via clues . You have a limited number of clues, represented by tokens like this: ​ clue tokens Each time a clue is given, one ​ clue tokens moves from the white area (available tokens) to the black (used tokens): ​ clue tokens ​ clue tokens ​ clue tokens ​ clue tokens ​ clue tokens ​ clue tokens ​ clue tokens ​ clue tokens ​ clue tokens ​ clue tokens ​ clue tokens ​ clue tokens ​ clue tokens ​ clue tokens ​ clue tokens 1 clue tokens 2 clue tokens 3 clue tokens 4 clue tokens 5 clue tokens 6 clue tokens 7 clue tokens 8 clue tokens . If there are no tokens available, you must play or discard on your turn. ​ Do not give information via chat. That is cheating. If you do, you are dishonored and your reputation as a master pyrotechnician is tainted. Setup In a 2-3 player game, each player gets a hand of 5 cards. In a 4-5 player game, each player gets a hand of 4 cards. Gameplay On your turn, you can do one of three things. Give a clue. Discard a card. Play a card. Give a Clue To give a clue, there must be at least 1 ​ clue tokens in the white area. Select another player's card. You have the choice of telling the player: Which cards of that color the player has Which cards of that number the player has At that point, 1 ​ clue tokens is moved from the white "available" zone to the black "used" zone. The game records these clues, so you can tell which cards other players have pointed out are what number and what color. Play a Card Select a card in your hand and then Play selected card or just drag the card onto the firework stacks in the center to play it. If it is the next card in sequence for a color, it is automatically placed on the appropriate stack, adding to or completing the firework stack. If it is not the next card in sequence for any color, then the firework has misfired and the card is discarded. A replacement card is automatically added to the left side of the player's hand. [Rating: 1/10] July 2019: Downgraded from 4 to 1. During one game, I was about to make a bad play and all the other players gasped. This actually upset me. Hanabi is a game of limited communication. If one player is about to screw up, you put up and go on. My opponents' excuse was, "but we're all gamers and we play to win."  Because of that experience, I will never play this game.  February 15, 2014: I really don't like co-operative games.  ==============================   Only play with non-gamers; they tend to get more into the spirit of the game (which are the rules), that is, only giving out information 

[Rating: 1/10] I think it really isn't a game. The overall goal seems to just set up the proper communication and then just see if it works. Like I said, not a game.

[Rating: 1/10] Hyperbole alert - I'd rather pin my hand to the dinner table with my fork than play this sordid combination of the worst elements of co-ops and Memory in a single gaming experience.  It's the Santorum of the game world.

[Rating: 1/10] Don't buy this, just have a try somewhere. Not so interesting as somebody told me, and I would not ever play again unless ... No unless.

[Rating: 1/10] Terrible game. It is extremely hard not to unintentionally cheat. You have to focus on remembering everything that has been said during the game which makes it frustrating to play. It is a coop that makes players annoyed at each other. They want you to keep score on how well you're doing but include no score sheet or anything with the game. It is also very random. One of the worst games I've ever played.

[Rating: 1/10] I bounced off of this game because having to make decisions based on only negative information is not a way that my brain wants to work.

[Rating: 1/10] Frustrating. Prefer card games where you engage in tactics and strategies rather than passively wait for clues (which you soon forget!)

[Rating: 1/10] Hanabi gave me anxiety, and totally bored my husband.  And this beat Augustus for game of the year? What were they thinking?

[Rating: 1/10] Too heavy for most if played properly, it tends to become an exercise in cheating.

[Rating: 1/10] Don't even bother playing if you have a hard time memorizing things.  The game is very susceptible to cheating.

[Rating: 1/10] Really don't know what should be so great watching people making deductions. If you want to fall asleep, this is the right game for you.

[Rating: 1/10] I like social interaction. I like games. However, I don't like games where social interaction is the only game mechanism. Stretching the boundaries between cheating and fair play is completely uninteresting to me. Hanabi defies my definition of a game. It feels more like a corporate retreat teambuilding activity or a childrens activity, and if viewed as such or as a psychosocial experiment/case study, it's fine, but if viewed as a game by a hobby gamer, it's among the absolut worst I've tried. [Rating: 1/10] We purchased the deluxe tile version of this game.  I don't recall us ever disliking a game more than this one.  It has a very heavy memory element which we both despise so it's my own fault I guess for not having researched it better.  Someone had described it as a better cooperative Code 777, but I like that game, or really any game at all more than Hanabi.  Past the memory element the rest of the gameplay is just dull.
